evidence_quotes.quote: This study, cross-sectional in design, was carried out over a three-year period (1 August 2011–31 July 2014) to assess the status of newer migrant households in the slums with regard to the provision of basic civic amenities. A simple random sample of 15 notified and 15 non-notified slum settlements was taken from a list of 50 notified and 41 non-notified slums obtained from the MCL.
All notified areas in a town or city notified as ‘Slum’ by State, Union territories Administration or Local Government under any Act including a ‘Slum Act’ are considered as Notified slums

There were clearly significant differences in the availability of basic amenities among those living in “notified” and “non-notified” slums or open spaces. The “notified” slums are those that are recognized by the municipal authorities, who are then obliged to provide basic civic amenities like water and sanitation to the residents.

Only 37.2 per cent of the households had piped water in their premises (45.4 per cent in notified and 35.3 per cent in non-notified slums). More than a quarter (26.7 per cent) of families living in open spaces had no water supply and purchased water from nearby sources
More than half (57.2 per cent) of the slum dwellers had no toilet facilities and resorted to open defecation; of those living in open spaces 83.3 per cent were open defecators (Table 4).

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to drinking water supply (in-house piped water, public tap, hand pump, or no water supply/purchasing water), sanitation/defecation facilities (own toilet at home, community toilet, mobile toilet, or open defecation), and drainage among urban slum migrant households in Ludhiana.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it examines legal and municipal governance factors shaping slum civic provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, the primary analytical stratification is statutory slum notification status ('notified slums' formally designated under a Slum Act vs. 'non-notified slums' and 'open spaces'), a legal/administrative recognition and tenure-linked eligibility rule under which municipal authorities are legally obliged to provide water and sanitation to notified slums while non-notified settlements face legal/institutional bottlenecks and lack of formal service entitlement. The study also documents household housing tenure and possession of identity/residence documentation (voter and ration cards).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical evidence from a cross-sectional survey of 3,947 newer migrant households across 30 randomly selected slum settlements (15 notified and 15 non-notified) conducted between August 2011 and July 2014, analysed using chi-square tests in SPSS.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports disaggregated household-level water and sanitation access outcomes across notified slums, non-notified slums, and open spaces (Table 4), including piped water at home, public tap, hand pump, lack of water supply (purchasing water), piped supply continuity (1-2 hours morning and evening), own toilet at home, community/mobile toilets, open defecation, and closed/open/absent drainage.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (household: 3,947 newer migrant households in 30 slum clusters in Ludhiana), exposure (statutory slum notification status: notified vs. non-notified slums and open spaces), outcome (household drinking-water, sanitation, and drainage access), and study design (cross-sectional cluster/purposive household survey) are all clearly defined and reported with complete contingency counts.

study_design: Cross-sectional household survey (random sample of 15 notified and 15 non-notified slum clusters with purposive/snowball sampling of newer migrant households)
population_and_sample: 3,947 newer migrant households (migrated >30 days and <10 years prior) across 30 randomly selected urban slum settlements (15 notified slums, n = 845; 15 non-notified slums, n = 3,072; and open spaces, n = 30) in Ludhiana, Punjab, North India (unit of analysis: household)
exposure: Statutory slum legal notification status (notified slums formally notified under a Slum Act vs. non-notified slums and unnotified open spaces governing municipal obligation to provide basic services), alongside housing tenure and identity/residence documentation (voter and ration cards)
outcome: Household drinking water supply access (piped water at home, public tap, hand pump, no water supply/purchasing water), sanitation facility access (own toilet at home, community toilet, mobile toilet, open defecation), and drainage availability (closed drain, open drain, no drainage)
rationale: This cross-sectional empirical survey of 3,947 migrant households in Ludhiana, India directly compares household drinking-water supply, toilet access/open defecation, and drainage across statutory slum notification categories (15 notified slums vs. 15 non-notified slums and open spaces). Because formal notification under a Slum Act is a rule-type legal/administrative classification that obliges municipal authorities to provide water and sanitation services and governs settlement eligibility for municipal infrastructure, the study satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2.
